content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper focuses on class-incremental, task-agnostic, and domain incremental settings in continual learning. It applies the idea of prompting (previously introduces in NLP) to continual learning over image transformer architecture. The main novelty (if I got this correctly) is the extension of prompt tuning to prompt pull and application to continual learning.
content.main_review:
The paper combines various mechanisms from previous works, but the details are not clear. The ideas sound similar to fast and slow learning weights (in few-show learning), including the key-value pair based query mechanism for dynamically selecting suitable prompts for different inputs. The paper says that keys are learnable, but I didn’t find how they are learned – eq. 3 performs selection using the cosine similarity between the query and keys, but it doesn’t say how the keys are obtained.
In experiments, the proposed method shows high accuracy compared to other tested methods. However, the paper claims that it compares to SOTA, while there are more recent works with higher performance.
content.summary_of_the_review: Due to incremental contribution, lack of details about the base methods and somewhat lacking benchmark, I cannot recommend acceptance.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

content.title: Response to Reviewer QXhJ
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for your detailed comments and constructive suggestions. We have tried to address all your comments in the following:

> The ideas sound similar to fast and slow learning weights (in few-show learning), including the key-value pair based query mechanism for dynamically selecting suitable prompts for different inputs. 

We would like to emphasize that our method is not a simple combination of prior work. Admittedly, the high-level concept of fast and slow learning is closely related to our idea. However, Complementary Learning Systems theory [1-2], the foundation of many continual learning methods, has also suggested the concept of fast and slow learning. Under this motivation, different methods have a very different way to achieve it for different challenges. Thus, we would like to argue that the similarity between our method and the fast and slow learning concept in few-shot learning could not be a reason for the lack of novelty. On the contrary, it exactly demonstrates the soundness of our method. Moreover, we are the first to introduce prompting into continual learning. And our method is far beyond trivial application, considering the fact prompt itself does not work for continual learning without our novel prompt pool structure and query mechanism.

> The paper says that keys are learnable, but I didn’t find how they are learned – eq. 3 performs selection using the cosine similarity between the query and keys, but it doesn’t say how the keys are obtained.

We have overloaded the definition of P in equation 3 with key-prompt pairs, thus keys are inside the objective. Nevertheless, we agree that this notation causes unnecessary confusion, and we will revise it in the next version.

> In experiments, the proposed method shows high accuracy compared to other tested methods. However, the paper claims that it compares to SOTA, while there are more recent works with higher performance.

We will add more baseline methods in our next version. However, the reason that we did not compare with more methods are included in the responses to Reviewer CrKX and y82g, please have a check.

[1] McClelland, James L., Bruce L. McNaughton, and Randall C. O'Reilly. "Why there are complementary learning systems in the hippocampus and neocortex: insights from the successes and failures of connectionist models of learning and memory." Psychological review 102.3 (1995): 419.

[2] Kumaran, Dharshan, Demis Hassabis, and James L. McClelland. "What learning systems do intelligent agents need? Complementary learning systems theory updated." Trends in cognitive sciences 20.7 (2016): 512-534.

content.summary_of_the_paper: Learning to Prompt (L2P) prepends a subset of learnable parameters (called prompts) from a larger set (called pool) to the input embeddings to learn tasks sequentially given a pretrained backbone model. The model was applied to various continual learning settings demonstrating better results than baselines.
content.main_review:
The related work section ignores numerous recent work in continual learning, especially closely related work such as:
- Joan Serrà, Dídac Surís, Marius Miron, and Alexandros Karatzoglou. Overcoming catastrophic forgetting with hard attention to the task. arXiv preprint arXiv:1801.01423, 2018.
- Loo, N., Swaroop, S., & Turner, R. E. (2020). Generalized variational continual learning. arXiv preprint arXiv:2011.12328.

The baselines in Tables 1-3 also ignore more recent stronger work.

The use of a fixed backbone is somewhat contentious because the main notion in continual learning is to continuously adapt the model. The 5-datasets experiments demonstrated that the model can adapt to different datasets. What about the heterogeneous case?
content.summary_of_the_review: Nice idea, missing related work, weak baselines, more experiments required to validate the fixed backbone in the model.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper3522 by Reviewer y82g

content.title: Response to Reviewer y82g
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for acknowledging the novelty of our idea and the valuable feedback. Here, we have carefully answered all your questions in the following:

> The related work section ignores numerous recent work in continual learning, especially closely related work such as...

We agree that these papers are related and will add them to our related work. Also, we would like to note that these methods mentioned use task identity at test time to retrieve task-specific components. This assumption (task-incremental setting) simplifies the continual learning problem. On the contrary, our method is able to automatically select task-specific information due to our novel key-value pair based query mechanism.

> The baselines in Tables 1-3 also ignore more recent stronger work.

We would like to point out that ER and GDumb are already very strong performing methods (see [1-2]) with a rehearsal buffer. Rehearsal-based methods are usually much stronger than methods without it. We mainly want to emphasize that our method is able to achieve competitive performance to rehearsal-based methods even without a rehearsal buffer, which is actually not a fair comparison to us and it is actually remarkable that our method can achieve it. However, we agree with the reviewer that stronger baselines can definitely make the result more convincing. So we will add more baselines and experiments in our next version.

> The use of a fixed backbone is somewhat contentious because the main notion in continual learning is to continuously adapt the model. The 5-datasets experiments demonstrated that the model can adapt to different datasets. What about the heterogeneous case?

Using a fixed backbone is actually quite standard in the prompt-tuning based works [3-4]. Our method re-targets at how to make the frozen models learn tasks sequentially, which is a different perspective from previous continual learning methods.


[1] Mai, Zheda, et al. "Online continual learning in image classification: An empirical survey." Neurocomputing 469 (2022): 28-51.

[2] Prabhu, Ameya, Philip HS Torr, and Puneet K. Dokania. "Gdumb: A simple approach that questions our progress in continual learning." ECCV 2020.

[3] Lester, Brian, Rami Al-Rfou, and Noah Constant. "The power of scale for parameter-efficient prompt tuning." arXiv preprint arXiv:2104.08691 (2021).

[4] Li, Xiang Lisa, and Percy Liang. "Prefix-tuning: Optimizing continuous prompts for generation." arXiv preprint arXiv:2101.00190 (2021).

[5] Rusu, Andrei A., et al. "Progressive neural networks." arXiv preprint arXiv:1606.04671 (2016).

content.summary_of_the_paper:
The paper presents the idea of prompting in the field of continual learning. Specifically, the author introduces an L2P framework that learns to dynamically prompt the model to learn tasks sequentially under different task transitions. To evaluate the proposed L2P, the paper conducts experiments under various settings.

Overall, the paper is well organized and clearly written. The proposed Learning to Prompt for Continual Learning (L2P) is quite straightforward and technically sound.
content.main_review:
Strengths:
1. The paper is the first to address continual learning with prompting techniques.

2. The proposed Learning to Prompt for Continual Learning (L2P) is technically sound. 

Weaknesses :
1. The baselines considered in this paper are too weak. Many latest methods are missing. Such as LoRA, K-Adapter, and other parameter-expansion methods.

2. The proposed Prompt Pool is similar to the idea of many memory-based continual learning methods. The paper should give more discussions and comparisons with these methods.

3.  This paper only experimented with visual-based data, and the results of language-based data could make the evaluation more convincing.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper is the first to address continual learning with prompting techniques, which makes sense to me.  The proposed L2P is also technically sound. However, the evaluation in this paper is a great concern to me. More strong baselines and more datasets can be included to make the evaluation more convincing. Besides, the paper should give more discussions and comparisons with the memory-based continual learning methods.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper3522 by Reviewer CrKX

content.title: Response to Reviewer CrKX
content.comment:
We sincerely thank the reviewer for these valuable comments. And we are encouraged to see your positive feedback on the novelty and technical soundness of the idea. We have tried to address your concern in the following response:

> The baselines considered in this paper are too weak. Many latest methods are missing. Such as LoRA, K-Adapter, and other parameter-expansion methods.

Firstly, we would like to emphasize that our method is a continual learning method, leveraging the idea of prompting, instead of a transfer learning method. Thus, comparing with transfer learning techniques, such as LoRA or K-Adapter is not an apple-to-apple comparison. Secondly, our method is not a direct application of prompting. It is our novel design of prompt pool and the query mechanism that make prompting compatible to the continual learning scenario. However, extending LoRA or K-Adapter to the continual learning setting is not trivial and beyond the scope of our work.

> The proposed Prompt Pool is similar to the idea of many memory-based continual learning methods. The paper should give more discussions and comparisons with these methods.

To our understanding, there are two types of “memory-based” continual learning methods: 1: rehearsal-buffer as the memory. 2. Task-specific component as the memory. We have compared with the first type (ER, GDumb) in our experiments, and it turns out in Table 1 that our method outperformed them when equipped with the same sized rehearsal buffer, and are strongly competitive when without a rehearsal buffer. While rehearsal based methods are not available when the buffer is absent. For the second type, task-specific components required test-time task identity to be retrieved (e.g., [1-2]), while our method does not require this information thanks to our novel query mechanism. Thus, these methods are based on easier assumptions and are not comparable to ours. Nevertheless, we agree with the reviewer that more strong baselines could make the evaluation more convincing. We will include more discussions and experiments in our next version.

> This paper only experimented with visual-based data, and the results of language-based data could make the evaluation more convincing.

Current continual learning works are mainly based on vision datasets, and the datasets used in our paper are widely recognized as challenging datasets in continual learning, albeit the simplicity of their i.i.d. version. However, we agree with the reviewer that adding language-based data would make the evaluation more convincing and would like to leave this direction as future work.

[1] Ke, Zixuan, Bing Liu, and Xingchang Huang. "Continual learning of a mixed sequence of similar and dissimilar tasks." NeurIPS 2020.

[2] Pham, Quang, Chenghao Liu, and Doyen Sahoo. "Contextual transformation networks for online continual learning." ICLR. 2020.
